origin: The doppelganger — a living person's exact double, seen where the person is not, and counted an omen of death. Grounded in German folklore (Doppelgänger) and the best-documented case: Emilie Sagée, a French teacher at a girls' school in Livonia in 1845, whose double was reported by pupils and staff to appear beside her, mimic her movements, and once sit at a table while she stood elsewhere — as recorded by Robert Dale Owen in Footfalls on the Boundary of Another World (1860). origin: The White Lady — a woman in white seen on a road or in a house, often a vanishing hitchhiker. Grounded in the widespread European White Lady folklore and its most famous American case: Resurrection Mary of Chicago, reported since the 1930s — a young woman in a white dress who asks for a ride on Archer Avenue, is driven to the Resurrection Cemetery gates, and vanishes; named for the cemetery where she is said to be buried. GHOST shelf.

In the European lore she haunts a house or a road and is bound to a tragedy — a lost love, a death in childbirth, an accident.

origin: The Dullahan — the headless rider of Irish folklore, carrying his own head under his arm and driving the black death coach. Grounded in Irish tradition (the dullahan as a harbinger of death, the Cóiste Bodhar as the silent black coach) and its most famous literary form: Washington Irving's Headless Horseman of Sleepy Hollow (The Legend of Sleepy Hollow, 1820), based on the Hessian trooper said to have lost his head in the Revolutionary War. origin: The Black Shuck — the spectral black hound of East Anglian folklore, an omen of death. Grounded in the most famous case: 4 August 1577, when a great black dog was reported to burst into the churches at Bungay and Blythburgh, Suffolk, during a storm, killing two people and scorching the church doors — an account recorded in A Straunge and Terrible Wunder (1577) and in the churches' own histories. GHOST shelf.

To meet it is an omen: in some tellings death follows within the year, in others it is a guardian, and the lore disagrees with itself on whether it is a warning or a threat.
